title: The Score for a Vanishing Sound
logline: A drumming teacher passes on a rhythm as spoken syllables before letting a student near the drum, a way of writing down, in sound, something that happens too fast to see.
human_question: How do you teach someone something that happens faster than it can be watched?

premise.story: A traditional drumming teacher in a village or town household teaches an apprentice a rhythm through spoken syllables, correcting and repeating until the pattern becomes automatic.
premise.place: A traditional drumming teacher's home or practice space.
premise.experience: The viewer watches an invisible, fast sequence become audible, memorable and eventually automatic, and feels what it takes to turn something too quick to grasp into something a person can learn and repeat.

concept_links.why: The source uses letter-symbols and dotted charts to make an invisible, extremely fast sequence of mind-moments memorable and recitable [C042-M:L3]. A drumming teacher's spoken syllables are a living, sonic version of exactly this kind of notation for something too fast to watch directly.

The source states that no single moment accomplishes an act; a whole series is required [C038-M:L3]. Watching a rhythm build up, beat by beat, in a student's hands makes that claim vivid without anyone naming it.

The source's picture of a trained response completing in a fast, unified burst describes what a rhythm looks like once an apprentice has fully learned it, in contrast to the halting, deliberate early attempts the film would also show.

what_camera_could_observe: The teacher reciting syllable patterns before any drum is touched
The student repeating them, correcting mistakes
Hands finally striking the drum, first haltingly, then more fluently
The teacher's hand keeping time and correcting in real time
A performance or ritual context where the learned rhythm is finally used
what_must_be_real: The teacher's real teaching method and the student's real pace of learning; no compressed or staged montage of progress that misrepresents how long real learning takes.

possible_arc.opening: A lesson begins with spoken syllables, no drum yet touched.
possible_arc.turn: A difficult passage, a repeated mistake, a real struggle to get it right.
possible_arc.ending_open: The rhythm is learned, or not yet, as honestly as the teaching actually goes.

position_hint: middle: a craft-and-teaching film that gives the group a strong sound-and-rhythm texture distinct from its other stories.

requirements: A traditional drumming teacher and apprentice household willing to be filmed over real lessons
Good sound recording conditions for the syllables and the drum
Consent that respects a hereditary tradition and does not exoticise it

suggestions.name: A traditional Kandyan drumming (bera) teaching household
suggestions.why: Kandy is closely associated with traditional drumming and its teaching lineages.
suggestions.verify: A specific teacher, student and willingness to be filmed are unconfirmed.

risks: Treating a living, hereditary art form as an illustration of doctrine rather than valuing it on its own terms
Exoticising a traditional teaching method for outside audiences
Compressing real learning time into a misleadingly fast montage
drop_if: No teacher and student are willing to be filmed over real lessons
The teaching method turns out not to use the described syllable-based approach
The tradition's keepers do not want it filmed or explained on camera

connections.note: Both make a fast, invisible sequence audible, spoken syllables for rhythm, a listening pause for language.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
